Nevertheless, this approach is not without its critics; some parties point out that differences in city and commercial zone size do not always correspond to population levels. Many factors can affect the extent of urban expansion such as topography and municipal annexation policies. Use of the base municipality's population in applying the population-mileage formula is also criticized. The corporate limits of many cities were established decades ago. Today, the population within many city limits is stagnant or declining, while the population in the suburbs is growing. It is argued that using only the base municipality's population leads to an inaccurate description of the commercial zone. Some parties assert that the corporate limits are often not readily ascertainable and suggest that the radius be measured from a named point in each city. Others foresee difficulties in determining whether or not a particular shipper is within the zone in instances where the outer boundary of the zone bisects an unincorporated community. The adviseability of making commercial zones, terminal areas, and exempt zones coterminal is also questioned. Finally, some parties assert that each commercial zone should be defined individually, at least for the larger cities. The Amercian Trucking Associations, Inc., suggests that zones be defined individually for all cities with populations of 100,000 or more.
